content: Consider the transverse field Ising model $d=1$ lattice and on the 4-8 lattice with both antiferromagnetic bonds as well as strong ferromagnetic bonds arranged such that every plaquette has a $\pi$ flux. For a large number of spins (i.e., more than $200$ spins) which of options have a provably efficient method for calculating the ground state properties of the models? a. DMRG for $d=1$ and QMC $d=2$ because QMC has no sign problem. b. Jordan-Wigner transformation for $d=1$ and QMC for $d=2$. c. No provably efficient method known in because QMC has sign problem $d=2$ and Jordan-Wigner transformation in $d=1$ d. QMC for $d=2$ because absence of sign problem and Jordan-Wigner transformation for $d=1$ e. Jastrow wavefunction for $d=1$ and no provably efficient method known in $d=2$. f. DMRG for $d=1$ and $d=2$. g. No provably efficient method known because lack of convergence guarantee of QMC even though there is no sign problem in $d=2$ and transfer matrix approach in $d=1$. h. No provably efficient method known QMC sign problem at low temperatures in $d=2$ and transfer matrix approach in $d=1$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Suppose you model a wavefunction of a quantum system with a recurrent neural network (RNN) out of which unbiased samples can be obtained. Within the framework of variational Monte Carlo, it is possible to estimate both the variational energy and the gradients of the energy with respect to the parameters $\lambda$ in the recurrent neural network wavefunction. The gradients of the energy are given by $\partial_{\lambda} E = \sum_{{\sigma},{\sigma'}} \partial_{\lambda} \left[ \psi^{*}_\lambda({\sigma}) H_{\sigma,\sigma'} \psi^{}_\lambda({\sigma'}) + \psi^{*}_\lambda({\sigma}) H_{\sigma,\sigma'} \partial_{\lambda} \psi^{}_\lambda({\sigma'})\right]$ A Monte Carlo estimator of the energy gradient is given by: $\partial_{\lambda} E \approx \frac{2}{N_S} \mathfrak{Re} \left ( \sum_{i=1}^{N_S} \frac{\partial_{\lambda}\psi^{*}_\lambda({\sigma^{(i)}})}{\psi^{*}_\lambda({\sigma^{(i)}})} E_{loc}({\sigma^{(i)}}) \right)$ where $N_s$ is the number of samples $\sigma^{(i)}$ drawn from the amplitude square of the RNN wavefunction. Which of the following statements is true: a. The gradient estimator is unbiased. b. The gradient estimator is biased because it misses a baseline involving the average energy. c. The gradient estimator is unbiased but has high variance. d. The gradient estimator is biased because in general the RNN and its gradients may have non-identical support in the computational basis. e. The gradient estimator is biased and has high variance. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a noninteracting time-reversal symmetric system of spin-1/2 fermions with a unique gapped ground state that has also four-fold rotation symmetry. Which rotation eigenvalues could the ground state have? (a) $+1$, (b) $e^{i \pi/4}$, (c) $i$, (d) $e^{i 3\pi/4}$, (e) $-1$, (f) $e^{-i 3 \pi/4}$, (g) $-i$, (h) $e^{-i \pi/4}$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a two-dimensional lattice system with 3x3 unit cells, where each unit cell consists of one site that can be empty, occupied by a spin-1/2 electron with either spin, or doubly occupied with two electrons of opposite spin. The system has periodic boundary conditions in both directions. The system has translation symmetry, time-reversal symmetry and fourfold rotation symmetry. We use all these symmetries (and no other) to block-diagonalize the Hamiltonian. How-many symmetry-distinct blocks exist, i.e., those not related to each other by a symmetry? Print your answer in a $\boxed{}$ LaTeX environment. Return your answer as plain text numbers separated by semicolons or commas when necessary (e.g., 1.23 or 1; 3).

Consider the following Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}= \sum\limits_{\langle \boldsymbol{r} \boldsymbol{r}' \rangle} \Big[ {J}_{z} S^{z}_{\boldsymbol{r}} S^{z}_{\boldsymbol{r}'} + { \frac{J_{\pm\pm}}{2}}( S^{+}_{\boldsymbol{r}} S^{+}_{\boldsymbol{r}'} + h.c. ) \Big] -h\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol{r} }S^{z}_{\boldsymbol{r}}$ defined on on the square and kagome lattices. Now consider their simulation via the stochastic series expansion (SSE) quantum Monte Carlo at some finite inverse temperature $\beta$. Which of the following statements is true: a. On the square lattice, the Hamiltonian has a sign problem. b. On the square lattice, the problem does not have a sign problem. c. On the kagome lattice, the model has a sign problem. d. Both on the square and kagome lattices, the model has a sign problem. e. Both on the square and kagome lattices, the model does not have as a sign problem. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a liquid composed by diatomic classical molecules in $d$ dimensions. Consider the problem of deriving an effective equation for the motion of one molecule In the limit $d\to\infty$. What is the appropriate cavity variable to be considered? Choose among the following: a - One tagged atom of a molecule b - One tagged molcule c - One tagged degree of freedom of the atom of a molecule. d - One tagged degree of freedom of the atom of a molecule, and one tagged degree of freedom of the partner atom in the same molecule. e - A cluster of molecules. f - None of the above. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a quantum Ising model at zero temperature with the following nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian: $H=-\sum_{i,j}\sigma^z_i\sigma^z_j + h\sum_i \sigma^x_i + g\sum_i \sigma^z_i$. Which of the following statements are correct? Indicate all that apply. a) At $h=1$ and $g=0$, the excitation energy vanishes. b) There is a symmetry breaking transition at a finite value of $h$. c) At $h=10$ and $g=1$, $\langle\sigma^z_{i}\sigma^z_{j}\rangle$ vanishes exponentially as a function of $|i-j|$. d) At $h=0.1$ and $g=1$, $\langle\sigma^x_{i}\sigma^x_{j}\rangle$ vanishes as a power-law for a large $|i-j|$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider the dynamics in two dimensions of the following modified active Brownian particle: $\mathbf{\dot x} = v_0 \mathbf{u}$, where $v_0$ is a postive constant, and $\mathbf{u}$ is a vector of unit norm, whose orientation $\theta$ with respect to the $x$ axis evolves according to the overdamped dynamics: $\dot\theta = -\frac{v_0}{T} \nabla V \cdot \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u} + \chi(t)$, where $V(\mathbf{x})$ is an external potential that depends only on $\mathbf{x}$, and $T$ is a positive constant. The matrix $\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix} 0&-1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ is a fully antisymmetric two-dimensional matrix. Consider a perturbation of the potential $V\to V + h(t)\phi(\mathbf{x})$. Cconsider the steady state linear response function $R(s) =\langle \frac{\delta \phi(\mathbf{x}(t+s))}{\delta h(t)}\rangle$ and the steady state autocorrelation function $C(s) = \langle \phi(\mathbf{x}(t))\phi(\mathbf{x}(t+s))\rangle$. Is the fluctuation dissipation theorem between these correlation and response functions violated? Choose one of the following options: (a) Yes, because the dynamics has a positive entropy production rate. (b) No, because the dynamics is time-reversible. (c) No, because the Boltzmann distribution is the stationary distribution. (d) Yes, because there is a nonzero self-propulsion speed. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider the Hamiltonian for spinless fermions on a 2D lattice at half-filling $H=-t \sum_{\langle i j\rangle}\left[c_i^{\dagger} c_j+H . c .\right] + V \sum_{\langle i j\rangle}\left(n_i-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(n_j-\frac{1}{2}\right)$ where $c_i^{\dagger}$ and $c_i$ are the creation and annihilation operators at site $i$, respectively, $n_i=c_i^{\dagger} c_i$ is the number operator and the sum $\langle i j \rangle$ runs over nearest-neighbor pairs of sites. Which of the following are correct? a. There is no sign problem for $V>0$. b. There is no sign problem for $V<0$. c. There is sign problem for $V>0$. d. There is sign problem for $V<0$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a tight binding model on a square lattice, whose sites are labeled by integers $x,y$. The Hamiltonian is given by $H=-t\sum_{x,y}c_{x,y}^{\dagger}c_{x,y+1}-t\sum_{x,y}e^{\frac{2i\pi y}{n}}c_{x,y}^{\dagger}c_{x+1,y}-t'\sum_{x,y}ie^{\frac{2i\pi y}{n}}\left(c_{x,y}^{\dagger}c_{x+1,y+1}+c_{x,y}^{\dagger}c_{x+1,y-1}\right)+h.c.$ with $n>1$ and real $t, t'$. Which of the following statements is true in the limit of an infinite system? a) The minimum of the lowest energy band is non-degenerate. b) The minimum of the lowest energy band is at least $n$ fold degenerate. c) The expectation value $\langle n_{x,y}\rangle$ of the density at site $x,y$ in the ground state with filling of $1/n$ particles per site is independent on $x,y$. d) The expectation value $\langle c^\dagger_{x,y} c_{x+1,y+1} \rangle$ is independent on $x,y$. e) The expectation value $\langle c^\dagger_{x,y} c_{x,y+1} \rangle$ is independent on $x,y$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

We are interested in counting fully packed dimer configurations on honeycomb lattice. Dimer can be placed on any of the nearest-neighbor bonds of the lattice and each site has to be a member of exactly one dimer. This is one of the ways to count ground state configurations of classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on triangular lattice. In particular, we want to consider a horizontal cylinder geometry, with the periodic boundary condition in vertical direction and zig-zag open edges. Here is an example of such geometry, given as an illustration in LateX's verbatim environment \begin{verbatim} \ / \ / A--B A--B / \ / \ B A--B A \ / \ / A--B A--B / \ / \ B A--B A \ / \ / A--B A--B / \ / \ B A--B A \end{verbatim} This is an XC-6 cylinder with width W=6, W being the number of sites in the vertical direction, and length L=3, again L being the number of honeycomb lattice unit cells in the horizontal direction. Let's call the number of "empty" sites divided by the total number of sites on the edge the "defect density". Answer following two questions. First, In the limit of wide cylinders, what defect density leads to the highest number of packed dimer configurations ? Second, for XC-11 cylinder, what is the defect density which gives the second highest number of packed dimer configurations ? Return your answer as plain text numbers separated by semicolons or commas when necessary (e.g., 1.23 or 1; 3).

Consider a two dimensional gappless quantum system with system size $L x L$, if one wants to solve the ground state of such system using DMRG and PEPS, how should the bond dimension scale with the system size respectively? The answer is expressed in terms of $L$ and nonzero constant c, $\alpha$: (a) $\chi_\text{DMRG}(L) \sim \exp(\alpha L), \; \chi_\text{PEPS}(L) \sim L^{c}$ (b) $\chi_\text{DMRG}(L) \sim L^{c}, \; \chi_\text{PEPS}(L) \sim \exp(c L)$ (c) $\chi_\text{DMRG}(L) \sim \exp(cL \log L), \; \chi_\text{PEPS}(L) \sim L^{c} \log L$ (d) $\chi_\text{DMRG}(L) \sim (L^{L})^c, \; \chi_\text{PEPS}(L) \sim L^{c}$ (e) $\chi_\text{DMRG}(L) \sim \exp(\alpha \log^2 L), \; \chi_\text{PEPS}(L) \sim \log^{c} L$ . Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model with nearest-neighbor coupling $J$ on a finite width $W$ and length $L$ cylinder on the square lattice with model Hamiltonian $H=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle } \vec{S}_i.\vec{S}_j$, where $i$ and $j$ are site indices, $\vec{S}_i$ is the spin operator on site $i$. The cylinder has open boundary condition along the length $L$ direction and periodic boundary condition along the width $W$ direction. Now let us compute the spin-spin correlation length in two different ways. First way is to directly calculate the spin-spin correlation function in the bulk of the system and extract the correlation length $\xi_1$ by using an exponential decaying function to fit the spin-spin correlation. Second way is to apply a small but finite staggered Zeeman pinning field (that is consistent with the antiferromagnetic pattern of the spin correlations) at the open boundary, and calculate how the absolute value of induced local staggered spin moment decays from the boundary to bulk using an exponential decaying function and extract the corresponding correlation length $\xi_2$. Now the question is when both width $W$ and length $L$ are finite and even numbers, what is the relation between $\xi_1$ or $\xi_2$? Choose from the following options:
(a) ξ_1 = ξ_2.
(b) ξ_1 > ξ_2 for any finite even cylinder.
(c) ξ_1 < ξ_2 for any finite even cylinder.
(d) ξ_1 diverges while ξ_2 remains finite.
(e) ξ_2 diverges while ξ_1 remains finite.
Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider the fermionic Hamiltonian \[ H = -t_1\sum_{i=1}^{N_u} (c^\dagger_{2i-1}c_{2i} + h.c.) -t_2\sum_{i=1}^{N_u-1} ( c^\dagger_{2i}c_{2i+1} + h.c.) \] For $t_2>t_1>0$, and at half filling, which of the following are true: a) This model has a topologically protected mode in the large-$N_u$ limit b) This model is topologically trivial in the large-$N_u$ limit c) The energy gap is of order $t_2(t_1/t_2)^2$ for small $t_1/t_2$ d) The energy gap is of order $t_1(t_2/t_1)^{N_u}$ for small $t_1/t_2$ e) The leading excitation is an ""end state"" localized on the end of the system f) The leading excitation is a ""bulk state"" that evenly occupies most sites of the system. Provide your answer in a $\boxed{}$ latex environment with a list of a subset of the letters a, b, c, d, e, and f, separated by a semicolon ;. For example $\boxed{a}$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

For the fermion Hamiltonian \[ H = \sum_{i=1}^n\left[\left(-tc_{i}^\dagger e^{iqa_{i,i+1}}c_{i+1}+h.c.\right)-\mu BS^z_i\right] \] where we have suppressed the spin index, $S^z_i$ is the usual spin operator for fermions, $B = \sum_ia_{i,i+1}$ is the magnetic field with $a_{i,i+1}$ classical parameters, and we have imposed periodic boundary conditions with the index arraned in a clockwise manner. Choose from the following options:
(a) A gauge transformation can remove the phase factors when qB is an integer multiple of 2π.
(b) The spectrum is independent of the magnetic flux B for any values of the parameters.
(c) Time-reversal symmetry is preserved for all choices of B and μ.
(d) The ground-state current vanishes identically for arbitrary B and μ.
(e) The Hamiltonian describes free fermions and can always be diagonalized by a Fourier transform without any flux dependence.
Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider the following Hamiltonian: $H=-J\sum_{j}c_{2j,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{2j+1,\sigma}-J'\sum_{j}c_{2j+1,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{2j+2,\sigma}+h.c.+g\sum_{j}n_{j\uparrow}n_{j\downarrow}$. The electron filling is $n=1/5$ per site. In the limit $g\rightarrow\infty$, and setting $J'=2J/3$, compute the equal time density-density correlation function $\langle n_{j}n_{j+r}\rangle$ for $j$ even and $r=0,1,2,3,4$. Give the answer with three digit accuracy. Return your answer as plain text numbers separated by semicolons or commas when necessary (e.g., 1.23 or 1; 3).

Consider a single-band fermionic spinful Hubbard model on a two-leg ladder on the square lattice, with model Hamiltonian $H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma} t_{ij} (c_{i\sigma}^+.c_{j\sigma}+h.c.) + U\sum_i n_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow}$, where $U>0$ is the on-site coulomb repulsion, $i$ and $j$ are site indices, $\sigma$ is the spin of an electron. $t_{ij}$ is the nearest-neighbor electron hopping integral, and takes the value $t_{ij}=t$ along the chain direction, and $t_{ij}=2t$ perpendicular to the chain direction. Now consider a case with electron filling $n=7/8$ per site, and $U=8t$, choose which one is its ground state from the options below (a) Luttinger liquid; (b) Luther-Emery liquid; (c) spin liquid; (d) non-Luttinger liquid. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider the transverse field ising model with antiferromagnetic interactions on the triangular lattice. Consider also the same model on the 4-8 lattice with both antiferromagnetic bonds as well as strong ferromagnetic bonds arrange such that every plaquette has a $\pi$ flux. Which of the following statements is true: a. The triangular lattice model has only one Kosterlitz-Thouless transition with emergent U(1) symmetry and the 4-8 lattice has an Ising transition at finite temperature. b. The 4-8 model has two Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions with emergent U(1) symmetry and the triangular lattice has two Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions at finite temperature with emergent U(1) symmetry. c. The 4-8 model has two Kosterlitz-Thouless transitions with emergent U(1) symmetry and the triangular lattice has an Ising transition at finite temperature. d. The 4-8 model has an Ising transition at finite temperature and the triangular lattice has an Ising transition at finite temperature. e. The 4-8 model has only one Kosterlitz-Thouless transition with emergent U(1) symmetry and the triangular lattice has an Ising transition at finite temperature. f. Both models exhibit order-by-disorder at zero temperature and a 3D Ising transition at high transverse field. g. Only the triangular model exhibits a transition to a spin liquid at high transverse field at zero temperature. h. No magnetically ordered phase arises in both models at zero temperature due to frustration. i. Both models have ordered phases at zero temperature. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a classical Ising model with the following Hamiltonian: $H= - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\ne j}J(|i-j|)\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}$, where $J(n)=|J_{0}|/(1+n^2)^{\alpha}$. Which of the following statements are correct? Indicate all that apply. a) For $\alpha=2$, there is a non-zero critical temperature $T_{c}$. b) For $\alpha=1$, at sufficiently low temperature, $\langle\sigma_{j}\sigma_{j+n}\rangle\rightarrow m^{2}>0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. c) For $\alpha=1$, there is a temperature for which $\langle\sigma_{j}\sigma_{j+n}\rangle-\langle\sigma_{j}\rangle\langle\sigma_{j+n}\rangle$ decays as the inverse of the logarithm of distance. d) For $\alpha=4$, $\langle\sigma_{j}\sigma_{j+n}\rangle$ decays exponentially with distance. e) For $\alpha=2$, $\langle\sigma_{j}\sigma_{j+n}\rangle$ decays exponentially with distance. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a two-dimensional model with attractive on-site interactions with the following Hamiltonian: $H=-\sum_{ij\sigma}t_{ij}(c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\textrm{H.c.}) - |U|\sum_i (n_{i\uparrow}-\frac{1}{2})(n_{i\downarrow}-\frac{1}{2})-\mu \sum_i n_i$, where $c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}$ ($c_{i\sigma}$) creates (annihilates) a fermion with spin $\sigma$ on site $i$, $n_{i\sigma}=c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{i\sigma}$ is the number operator, $t_{ij}$ is the amplitude of the hopping between sites $i$ and $j$ ($i\neq j$), $|U|>0$ is the strength of attraction between fermions on the same site, $\mu$ is the chemical potential, and $n_i=(n_{i\uparrow}+n_{i\downarrow})$ is the total particle number operator on site $i$. Assume that the electron filling is $\langle n\rangle=0.12$. Which of the following statements are correct? Indicate all that apply. a) The ground-state at $T=0$ is always a superconductor regardless of ratio of $t/U$. b) For $|U|\gg t$, the superconducting transition temperature behaves as $t$. c) For $|U|\gg t$, the superconducting transition temperature behaves as $t^2/|U|$. d) For $|U|\ll t$, the superconducting transition temperature behaves as $|U|$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

We want to build infinite two-dimensional tensor network wavefunction for a systems of spin-1 moments on square lattice interacting with SU(2)-symmetric interactions. We choose infinite projected entangled-pair state as the TN. We want to guarantee, that our TN respects i) translational symmetry of the lattice, ii) SU(2) symmetry of the interactions, and iii) symmetry of the lattice under rotations, C_4. A simplest choice is to generate the TN from a single 5-dimensional tensor $T_{puldr}$, with one physical index, $p$, corresponding to spin-1 physical degree of freedom and four virtual spaces V, labeled by indices $u$, $l$, $d$, and $r$, associated the up, left, down, and right directions on the lattice. We want tensor T to be invariant under the action of both spin-SU(2) and lattice rotations. Let's describe the action of SU(2) symmetry and lattice rotations: The SU(2) group acts on the tensors as $g(T) \rightarrow W(g)_{pp'} U(g)_{uu'} U(g)_{ll'} U(g)_{dd'} U(g)_{rr'} T_{p'u'l'd'r'} = T_{puldr}$ with U and W being appropriate matrix representations of SU(2) group. The group of lattice rotations acts on T by permutation (clockwise or anticlockwise) of its virtual indices, i.e. rotation by 90 degrees clockwise corresponds to $R(-\pi/2})(T_{puldr}) = T_{pruld}$. We choose the virtual spaces (indexed by u,l,d, and r) to be all identical and each composed from a direct sum of $V= 0 \oplus 1$ i.e. a direct sum of trivial irrep of SU(2) and spin-1 irrep of SU(2). How many (real-valued) variational parameters would our TN wavefunction have ? That is, how many independent tensors T_{puldr}, transforming under A irrep of the C_4 group of rotations and invariant under SU(2) group do we need to consider ? Return your answer as plain text numbers separated by semicolons or commas when necessary (e.g., 1.23 or 1; 3).

The following systems have degenerate ground states in the thermodynamic limit. Which of them have exactly degenerate ground states even in finite size systems? (a) Heisenberg ferromagnet, (b) Heisenberg antiferromagnet, (c) Laughlin states from Coulomb interaction in the lowest Landau level on the torus geometry, (d) Moore-Read states from Coulomb interaction in the second Landau level on the torus geometry, (e) Transverse field Ising model in the ferromagnetic phase. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider a $S=1$ Hamiltonian on a honeycomb lattice, $\mathbf{H}=-\sum_{\langle i, j\rangle_x} \mathbf{S}_i^x \mathbf{S}_j^x- \sum_{\langle i, j\rangle_y} \mathbf{S}_i^y \mathbf{S}_j^y- \sum_{\langle i, j\rangle_z} \mathbf{S}_i^z \mathbf{S}_j^z$ and an unitary operator $\mathbf{U}^\gamma=e^{i \pi \mathbf{S}^{\gamma }}$. Consider an operator defined on a plaquette $p$, $W_p=(-1)^{2 S} \mathbf{U}_1^z \mathbf{U}_2^x \mathbf{U}_3^y \mathbf{U}_4^z \mathbf{U}_5^x \mathbf{U}_6^y$ where the subscripts indicate the sites on the hexagonal plaquette $p$. $W_p$ commutes the Hamiltonian. Also consider an operator defined on a loop $LG$, $Q_{\mathrm{LG}}=\operatorname{tTr} \prod_\alpha Q_{k_\alpha i_\alpha j_\alpha}^{s s^{\prime}}|s\rangle\left\langle s^{\prime}\right|$, where $s$ and $s^\prime$ are spin indices and $k_\alpha, i_\alpha, j_\alpha ={0,1}$ are virtual bond indices. $Q_{\mathrm{LG}}$ is a projector satisfying $W_p Q_{\mathrm{LG}}=Q_{\mathrm{LG}} W_p=Q_{\mathrm{LG}}$. Which of the following are correct ? (a) $\mathbf{Q}_{000}=\mathbf{I}$ (b) $\mathbf{Q}_{011}=\mathbf{U}^z$ (c) $\mathbf{Q}_{101}=i\mathbf{U}^x$, (d) $ \mathbf{Q}_{110}=i\mathbf{U}^y$, (e) $\mathbf{Q}_{111}=\mathbf{U}^z$, (f) $\mathbf{Q}_{002}= -i\mathbf{U}^x$. Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Consider spin-polarized electrons in a lowest Landau level of a finite system with square aspect ratio and periodic boundary conditions that is penetrated by $4N$ quanta of magnetic flux at quarter filling, that interact via the Coulomb interaction. We are interested in the scaling of the spacing between consecutive energy levels with $N$ as $N$ becomes large. Which of the following scaling relations can be found among the 20 lowest energy eingenvalues? (a) $O(1)$, (b) $O(1/N)$, (c) $O(1/N^2)$, (d) $O(e^-N)$, (e) exact degeneracy? Return your answer as a semicolon-separated list of the chosen option letters (e.g., a; c; d).

Suppose that we want to perform exact diagonalization of a Hamiltonian for a kagome lattice model with only nearest-neighbor interactions and local terms. What is the maximum number of isomorphically distinct connected 5-site clusters that can be considered? Give the final answer in a $\boxed{}$ LaTeX environment. Return your answer as plain text numbers separated by semicolons or commas when necessary (e.g., 1.23 or 1; 3).

Consider a two-dimensional tight-binding model on the square lattice with a single orbital at each site. The lattice vectors are along $x$ and $y$ directions. Label each site by its coordinate $\vec{r}=(n_x,n_y)$ with two integers $n_x,n_y$. The model has nearest neighbor hopping $t_1$ along $x$ direction. Along $y$ direction the nearest neighbor hopping is $t_2$ for $n_x+n_y$ even, and $t_2e^{i\theta}$ for $n_x+n_y$ odd. For $t_1=t_2=1,\theta=\pi/3$, and chemical potential $\mu=0.1,0.3,1.2$, how many connected segments are there in the fermi surface, respectively? Present the final answer of the three integers in a single $\boxed{}$ LaTeX environment. For example: $\boxed{1,2,3}$. Given the following single-particle Hamiltonian in the second quantization formalism as \begin{equation} \hat{\mathcal{H}}_0=\sum_{\tau={\pm}} \int d^2 \bm{r} \Psi_{\tau}^\dagger(\bm{r}) H_{\tau} \Psi_{\tau}(\bm{r}), \end{equation} \begin{equation} H_{\tau}=\begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\hbar^2\bm{k}^2}{2m_\mathfrak{b}}+\Delta_{\mathfrak{b},\tau}(\bm{r}) & \Delta_{\text{T},\tau}(\bm{r})\\ \Delta_{\text{T},\tau}^\dag(\bm{r}) & -\frac{\hbar^2\left(\bm{k}-\tau \bm{\kappa}\right)^2}{2m_\mathfrak{t}}+ \Delta_\mathfrak{t,\tau}(\bm{r}) \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \Psi_{+}(\bm{r})=\begin{pmatrix} \psi_{\mathfrak{b},\uparrow,+}(\bm{r}) \ \\ \psi_{\mathfrak{t},\downarrow,+}(\bm{r}) \end{pmatrix}, \quad \Psi_{-}(\bm{r})=\begin{pmatrix} \psi_{\mathfrak{b},\downarrow,-}(\bm{r}) \ \\ \psi_{\mathfrak{t},\uparrow,-}(\bm{r}) \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} where $\tau=\pm $ represents $\pm K$ valleys, $\hbar \bm{k} = -i \hbar \partial_{\bm{r}}$ is the momentum operator, $\bm{\kappa}=\frac{4\pi}{3a_M}\left(1,0\right)$ is at a corner of the moir'e Brillouin zone, and $a_M$ is the moir'e lattice constant.
